title: Catabolism of Carbon Skeletons of Amino Acids (Part 2)
objectives: Trace the catabolic pathways of amino acids to succinyl-CoA, pyruvate, and acetyl-CoA
Understand disorders of branched-chain amino acid metabolism
Explain clinical manifestations and management of metabolic disorders

succinyl_coa.title: Amino Acids Yielding Succinyl-CoA
succinyl_coa.content:
Succinyl-CoA Producers (VIMT)

1. Methionine (M)

  • Activated to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
  • Donates methyl group → S-adenosylhomocysteine

2. Threonine (T)

  • Threonine dehydratase → α-ketobutyrate (PLP/NADPH)
  • Converted to propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA

pyruvate.title: Amino Acids Yielding Pyruvate
pyruvate.content:
Pyruvate Producers (SCWATG)

1. Alanine (A)

  • Direct transamination with α-KG → pyruvate
  • No known defects

2. Tryptophan (W)

  • Side chain cleaved to alanine → pyruvate

3. Serine (S)

  • Serine dehydratase → pyruvate (PLP/NADPH)

4. Glycine (G)

  • Pathway 1: Glycine ↔ serine → pyruvate
  • Pathway 2: Glycine cleavage system (CO2 + NH4+ + CH2-THF)
  • Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia: Glycine accumulation (neuroinhibitory)
  • Pathway 3: Glyoxylate → oxalate → kidney stones

Cysteine Disorders

  • Cystinosis: Cysteine transport defect → tissue deposits
  • Cystinuria: Renal reabsorption defect (CORK amino acids)
  • Homocystinuria: Cystathionine β-synthase defect (B6-responsive)
  • High homocysteine → cardiovascular risk

acetyl_coa.title: Amino Acids Yielding Acetyl-CoA
acetyl_coa.content:
Acetyl-CoA Producers (FLY TWIK)

1. Lysine (K)

  • Exclusively ketogenic
  • Yields crotonyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA (via β-oxidation)

2. Tryptophan (W)

  • Kynurenine pathway → α-ketoadipate → acetyl-CoA

bcaa.title: Branched-Chain Amino Acid Catabolism
bcaa.content:
BCAA Metabolism (Leu, Ile, Val)

Degradation Steps

  • 1. Transamination to α-ketoacids
  • 2. Oxidative decarboxylation (BCKD complex)
  • 3. Dehydrogenation (similar to FA oxidation)

Metabolic Fates

  • Leucine: Acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate (ketogenic)
  • Isoleucine: Acetyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA (amphibolic)
  • Valine: Methylmalonyl-CoA (glucogenic)

Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)

Types

  • Classic: Neonatal onset, lethal without treatment
  • Intermittent: 30% BCKD activity, later onset

Clinical Features

  • Maple syrup odor urine (leucine derivatives)
  • Neurological impairment, ketoacidosis
  • Mental retardation if untreated

Management

  • BCAA-restricted diet
  • Synthetic formula supplementation
  • Tandem mass spectrometry (TMS) screening

Isovaleric Acidemia

  • Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase defect
  • Leucine catabolism block
  • Acidosis, vomiting after protein intake

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does MSUD cause neurological symptoms? +

A: Elevated leucine and its ketoacid compete with other neutral amino acids for brain transport, disrupting neurotransmitter synthesis and myelin formation.

Q: How does vitamin B6 help some homocystinuria patients? +

A: B6 is a cofactor for cystathionine β-synthase. Some mutant enzymes retain partial activity when saturated with B6, improving homocysteine metabolism.

Q: Why are BCAA catabolized in extrahepatic tissues? +

A: Liver lacks BCAA transaminases, directing these amino acids to muscles and other tissues where their carbon skeletons are important energy sources.
